“The way the first man runs, he looks like Ahimaaz, Zadok’s son,” the lookout said. “He is a good man,” said the king. “His news will be good.”

Ahimaaz called to the king, “Peace!”{l} He knelt, touching his forehead to the ground. “Blessed be Yahweh your God,” he said. “He has delivered to you the men who lifted their fists against my lord the king.”
“And is young Absalom safe?” the king asked. Ahimaaz said, “When Joab sent me, there was a great commotion, but I did not find out what it meant.”
“Step aside and wait here,” the king said. So Ahimaaz stepped aside and stood there.
Then the man from Cush arrived. “Good news for my lord the king!” he said. “Today Yahweh has given you justice against everyone who fought you.”
The king questioned the Cushite, “What about young Absalom? Is he safe?” The Cushite said, “Let every enemy of my lord the king, and everyone who rises to harm you, share that young man’s fate.”

The king was shaken to the core. He climbed to the room over the gateway and sobbed. As he went, he moaned, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son! Why was it not me who died instead of you? Absalom, my son, my son!”{m}

notes.text: So two Hebrew copies, the Greek Old Testament, and the Latin Vulgate (reported). The traditional Hebrew text reads “for now there are ten thousand like us.”
The forest of Ephraim was east of the Jordan, in Gilead, in spite of its name.
So the Greek Old Testament and other ancient versions (reported). The Hebrew reads “he was set.”
Hebrew “ten of silver,” that is, ten shekels, about 4 ounces (115 grams).
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms).
So some Hebrew copies and ancient versions (reported), which read “for me.” The traditional text reads “whoever you are.”
So the written Hebrew text. The traditional reading is “my life.”
Hebrew “three sticks” or “three rods,” perhaps spears or javelins.
Compare 14:27, which says Absalom had three sons. Perhaps they died young.
Cush was the region south of Egypt (Nubia).
That is, the plain of the Jordan Valley.
Hebrew “Shalom,” meaning “Peace” or “All is well.”
In Hebrew this verse is 19:1, so English 19:1-43 is Hebrew 19:2-44. The Greek Old Testament follows the Hebrew numbering.

verses.text: Someone informed Joab that the king was weeping and grieving over Absalom.{a}
So the joy of that victory turned into sorrow for the whole army, because the soldiers kept hearing that the king was heartbroken over his son.
That day the men slipped quietly into the city, like soldiers sneaking home in shame after running from a battle.
The king had covered his face. He kept wailing, “My son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!”

Joab entered the house where the king was and told him, “You have humiliated your entire staff today. These are the very men who kept you alive, along with your sons and daughters, your wives, and your concubines.

You care for those who despise you and despise those who care for you! Today you have shown that commanders and common soldiers are nothing to you. It is clear to me that Absalom’s survival would please you, even if all of us lay dead.

Now stand up, go out, and speak warmly to your men. I promise by Yahweh that if you stay in here, not one man will remain at your side by nightfall. That disaster would be worse than every one you have suffered from your youth until now.”
The king stood up and sat down in the gateway. When the news went around, “The king is at the gate,” everyone came before him. The Israelites, for their part, had fled, each man to his own home.
All over the tribes of Israel, people debated. “The king saved us from our enemies and delivered us from the Philistines,” they said. “Yet now he has left the country because of Absalom.
Absalom, the one we anointed as our ruler, is dead from the fighting. So what is holding you back from welcoming the king home?”

Through Zadok and Abiathar the priests, David sent this word: “Speak to the leaders of Judah. Say, ‘Will you be the last tribe to escort your king to his palace? What all Israel is saying has already come to the king in his quarters.{b}
You are my kin, my bones and my body. So why would you be the final ones to bring me back?’
Say to Amasa also, ‘You are my own flesh and blood. May God strike me down, and worse, if I fail to make you commander of my army permanently in Joab’s place.’”
In this way David moved the hearts of all the men of Judah so that they agreed together. They sent the king this word: “Return, you and all those who serve you.”
So the king set out for home and reached the Jordan. Judah’s men had assembled at Gilgal to go out and meet him and bring him across the river.
Shimei, Gera’s son, the Benjamite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand Benjamites came with him. Ziba, the servant of Saul’s household, came too, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants. They splashed into the Jordan before the king arrived.
They crossed at the ford,{c} ready to ferry the royal household over and to serve the king however he wished. As the king was about to cross, Shimei fell flat on the ground in front of him.
He pleaded, “My lord, please do not hold my guilt against me. Forget the shameful thing I did the day you left Jerusalem. Do not let it weigh on you.
I know I have sinned. That is why I came today. I am the first from all the tribes descended from Joseph to come down and welcome my lord the king.”
Abishai, Zeruiah’s son, spoke up: “Should Shimei not die for this? He cursed Yahweh’s anointed king!”

David said, “Sons of Zeruiah, what business do you have with me? Why are you working against me{d} today? Is anyone going to be put to death in Israel today? I know very well that I am Israel’s king again.”
Then the king said to Shimei, “You will not die.” He made a solemn promise to him.

Mephibosheth, the grandson of Saul, also went down to meet the king. Since the king’s departure, and all the way to his safe return, Mephibosheth had neglected his feet, left his mustache untrimmed, and never laundered his clothes.
When he came from Jerusalem{e} to see the king, the king asked him, “Mephibosheth, what kept you from going with me?”
He answered, “My lord the king, my servant tricked me. I had told him, ‘Saddle my donkey so I can ride and go with the king,’ because I cannot walk well.
He has also slandered me to my lord the king. But my lord has the wisdom of an angel of God. Do what you think best.
My whole family deserved death from my lord the king, yet you gave me a seat among those who eat at your table. What more can I claim? Why should I make any further appeal to the king?”
The king said, “You do not need to say any more. Here is my decision: you and Ziba will split the property.”
Mephibosheth said, “Let him have it all. The only thing that matters is that my lord the king has come home safe.”
Barzillai the Gileadite had traveled down from Rogelim. He accompanied the king as far as the Jordan, to bid him farewell at the crossing.
Barzillai was elderly, a man of eighty. He was also very rich, and he had supplied the king with food during his time at Mahanaim.
The king invited Barzillai, “Cross with me, and I will look after you while you live in Jerusalem.”
Barzillai answered the king, “How much longer will I live? Is it worth going up to Jerusalem with the king?

I am eighty years old now. Can I judge between good and bad anymore? Can my tongue savor food and drink? Can my ears still enjoy the voices of singers, both men and women? Why should your servant become a weight on my lord the king?
I would go only a short way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king reward me like that?

Let me turn back, so I may die in my hometown and be laid next to my father and mother. But Chimham,{f} your servant, is here. Let him cross with my lord the king, and do for him whatever you think is good.”
The king agreed: “Chimham will go with me, and I will treat him the way you would like. I will also do for you anything you ask.”
So all the people crossed the Jordan, and then the king crossed. He kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal, with Chimham beside him. The entire army of Judah and half the army of Israel took the king across.

Before long, all the men of Israel approached the king and protested, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, steal you away? They escorted the king, his household, and all David’s men over the Jordan!”
The men of Judah shot back, “We are the king’s close kin! Why are you so upset? Have we lived off the king? Did he hand us any presents?”

The men of Israel retorted, “We hold ten parts of the king, so David is more ours than yours.{g} Why did you look down on us? Were we not the ones who first proposed returning our king?” But the men of Judah answered even more sharply than the men of Israel had.

notes.text: This is Hebrew 19:2. English 18:33 is Hebrew 19:1, so English 19:1-43 is Hebrew 19:2-44. The Greek Old Testament follows the Hebrew numbering.
The Hebrew puts “what all Israel is saying has reached the king” at the end of the verse. The sentence is hard to follow and is reordered here.
The Hebrew is unclear. Perhaps “the ferryboat crossed over.”
Or “a satan,” that is, an accuser or opponent.
Or “came to Jerusalem.”
Chimham probably means “longing” (uncertain). He seems to have been Barzillai’s son (compare 1 Kings 2:7).
The Greek Old Testament reads “we are older than you.” Some scholars prefer “we are the firstborn rather than you.”

verses.text: A troublemaker{a} named Sheba,{b} the son of Bichri, a man of Benjamin, was standing nearby. He sounded a ram’s horn and yelled, “We have no share in David! We get nothing from the son of Jesse! Every man go home, Israel!”
So all the Israelite men abandoned David and followed Sheba, Bichri’s son. The men of Judah, however, stayed close to their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David arrived at his palace in Jerusalem. The ten concubines he had left in charge of the house were moved by his order into a guarded house. He provided for them, but he never visited their beds again. They stayed locked up until the day they died, living as if their husband were dead.
The king ordered Amasa, “Call up the men of Judah to assemble in three days, and be here yourself.”
Amasa set out to gather Judah, but he took longer than the time David had set.
David told Abishai, “Sheba, Bichri’s son, will now be more dangerous to us than Absalom was. Take my officers and chase him, or he may reach fortified cities and slip out of our reach.”{c}
Joab’s men went out after Abishai, along with the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the other fighters. They marched from Jerusalem to hunt down Sheba, Bichri’s son.
They were at the great rock in Gibeon when Amasa approached them. Joab had on his soldier’s tunic, and strapped around it was a belt with a sheathed sword. As he walked forward, the blade fell out.
Joab asked Amasa, “How are you, brother?” He reached out with his right hand and grabbed Amasa’s beard, pretending to greet him with a kiss.

Amasa did not watch the sword in Joab’s other hand. Joab plunged it into Amasa’s stomach, and his insides poured onto the ground. No second stroke was needed. Amasa was dead. Joab and his brother Abishai then kept on after Sheba, Bichri’s son.
A young soldier of Joab’s stood beside Amasa’s body and shouted, “Anyone who favors Joab, anyone who is on David’s side, follow Joab!”
Amasa was writhing in his own blood on the highway. The young man noticed that everyone who came along stopped to look. So he pulled the body into a field and threw a cloak over it.
Once the body was off the road, everyone moved on behind Joab to chase Sheba, Bichri’s son.
Sheba traveled through all the tribes of Israel until he reached Abel Beth-maacah.{d} All the Bichrites{e} came together and followed him into the town.
Joab’s forces came and trapped Sheba in Abel Beth-maacah. They built a ramp of earth against the city, level with its outer wall, and the whole army with Joab battered the wall to knock it down.
A clever woman called out from the city, “Hear me, hear me! Ask Joab to step over here. I want to speak with him.”
He came up to her, and she asked, “Are you Joab?” “Yes,” he said. “Hear your servant’s words,” she said. “Go ahead,” he replied.
She said, “People used to say long ago, ‘Get your answer at Abel.’ And that was how disputes ended.{f}
I am from the quiet, faithful families of Israel. You want to wipe out a city that is a mother to Israel’s towns. Why would you gulp down Yahweh’s own possession?”
“Never!” Joab answered. “I have no wish to swallow up or destroy anything!

No, that is not it. Sheba son of Bichri, from the hills of Ephraim, has turned against King David. Hand over that single man, and I will withdraw from the city.” “Understood,” the woman said. “His head will come flying to you over the wall.”

The woman went to all the people with her wise plan. They beheaded Sheba son of Bichri and flung the head to Joab. He blew the ram’s horn, and the troops scattered from the city to their homes. Joab returned to the king at Jerusalem.
Joab was commander of all Israel’s army. Benaiah, Jehoiada’s son, was in charge of the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram{g} supervised the forced labor, and Jehoshaphat, Ahilud’s son, was the royal historian.
Sheva was the secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira from the clan of Jair{h} also served David as a priest.

notes.text: Hebrew “a man of Belial,” meaning a worthless person.
Sheba probably means “seven” or “oath” (uncertain). Bichri probably means “youthful” or “firstborn” (uncertain).
The Hebrew is unclear. Literally, “and snatch away our eye.” The Greek Old Testament reads “so he will blind our eyes.”
Abel Beth-maacah means “meadow of the house of Maacah.” It was in the far north.
So the Hebrew. Some ancient versions read “Berites” or “all the choice men.”
The Greek Old Testament has a longer saying about asking in Abel and in Dan whether the faithful in Israel had come to an end. Some scholars think “and in Dan” is original.
Adoram is a short form of Adoniram (1 Kings 4:6), which is what the Greek Old Testament reads.
Hebrew “the Jairite.” The Greek Old Testament reads “Iras, son of Iarin.” Jair was a leader in the tribe of Manasseh (Numbers 32:41).

verses.text: During David’s reign, three years of famine struck, one after another. David sought an answer from Yahweh. Yahweh said, “Saul and his murderous household are to blame. He killed the Gibeonites.”

The king summoned the Gibeonites. (They were not Israelites. They were survivors of the Amorites. Israel had sworn an oath to spare them,{a} but Saul, burning with zeal for Israel and Judah, had tried to exterminate them.) David spoke with them.
David said, “What should I do for you? How can I make amends so that you will bless Yahweh’s people?”
They answered, “Silver and gold cannot settle this between us and Saul’s family. And we have no right to execute anyone in Israel.” “Then what do you want?” David asked. “I will do it.”
They told the king, “Saul was the man who destroyed us and schemed to remove us from every part of Israel.
Give us seven of his sons, and we will hang them{b} before Yahweh at Gibeah, Saul’s town, the man Yahweh chose.”{c} “I will hand them over,” the king said.
The king did protect Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, because of the promise before Yahweh between David and Jonathan, Saul’s son.

But he took two sons Rizpah, Aiah’s daughter, had borne to Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, and the five sons of Saul’s daughter Merab.{d} Merab had borne them to Adriel, the son of Barzillai from Meholah.

David gave these seven into the hands of the Gibeonites, who hanged them on the hill before Yahweh. All seven died together. They were put to death in the first days of the harvest, when the barley harvest was beginning.{e}

Rizpah, Aiah’s daughter, laid out sackcloth for herself on the rock face. From the beginning of the harvest until the rains came down on the bodies, she kept watch. She would not allow birds of the sky to perch on them in the day, or wild animals to approach at night.
Someone reported to David what Rizpah, Aiah’s daughter and Saul’s concubine, was doing.

David then went to the leaders of Jabesh-gilead and collected the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan. Those people had stolen them from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had displayed the bodies after killing Saul on Gilboa.
From there David carried away the remains of Saul and Jonathan. The bones of the seven who were hanged were gathered up as well.

The bones of Saul and Jonathan were buried in Zela,{f} in Benjamin’s land, in the family tomb of Saul’s father, Kish. All the king’s orders were completed. After this, God responded to the prayers on behalf of the land.
The Philistines fought Israel once more. David led his men down to battle, but he grew faint.
Ishbi-benob,{g} one of the descendants of the giants,{h} had a bronze spearhead weighing about 7½ pounds,{i} and he wore a new belt or weapon.{j} He planned to kill David.

But Abishai, Zeruiah’s son, came to David’s rescue and struck the Philistine dead. Then David’s men made him swear: “You will never again go out to battle with us. You must not let the lamp of Israel go out.”
Later there was a second clash with the Philistines, at Gob. Sibbecai of Hushah struck down Saph, who was also of the giants’ line.
A third clash with the Philistines happened at Gob. Elhanan, the son of Jaare-oregim of Bethlehem, killed Goliath of Gath,{k} a man whose spear had a shaft like a weaver’s beam.
A fourth fight broke out at Gath. A giant of a man lived there with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in total. He was another of the giants’ line.
He mocked Israel, and Jonathan, the son of David’s brother Shimei,{l} killed him.
These four men were descendants of the giants of Gath, and they died at the hands of David and his men.

notes.text: See Joshua 9:3-27.
It is not clear how they were executed. Perhaps “impaled” or “left exposed.” The same applies to verses 9 and 13.
So the Hebrew. Some scholars change it to “on the mountain of Yahweh” (compare verse 9). The Greek Old Testament reads “in Gibeon of Saul, as chosen for the Lord.”
So two Hebrew copies and some Greek copies (compare 1 Samuel 18:19). Most Hebrew copies read “Michal.” Armoni probably means “of the palace” (uncertain).
Barley harvest came in April and May.
Zela probably means “rib” or “side” (uncertain).
Ishbi-benob probably means “his dwelling is in Nob” (uncertain).
Hebrew “the Rapha,” the ancestor of a race of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11). The same applies to verses 18, 20, and 22.
Hebrew “three hundred shekels,” about 7½ pounds (3.4 kilograms).
The Hebrew says “he was belted with new,” and the noun is missing. The Greek Old Testament reads “with a club.”

First Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath of Gath. Compare 1 Samuel 17, where David kills Goliath. The word “Oregim” means “weavers” and may have been copied by mistake from the end of the verse. Scholars still debate this.
So the traditional reading (qere). The written text reads “Shimei.” Elsewhere he is called Shimeah (13:3) or Shammah (1 Samuel 16:9).

verses.text: David sang this song to Yahweh after Yahweh had freed him from every enemy, and from Saul.{a}
He sang: “Yahweh is a mountain crag to me, a stronghold, and the one who sets me free.

My God is my rock, and I hide in him.
He is my shield, my mighty horn,{b}
my tower on the heights, my place to run.
My savior, you keep me safe from violent people.

I call to Yahweh, who deserves all praise,
and I am saved from those who hate me.

Waves of death crashed around me.
Floods of destruction{c} terrified me.

The ropes of the grave{d} wound around me.
Death set traps right in my path.

In my distress I cried out to Yahweh.
I shouted for help to my God.
In his temple he listened to me,
and my plea came to his ears.

The earth shook and swayed.
The foundations of the sky trembled and rocked,
because he was burning with anger.

Smoke poured from his nose,
and a devouring fire from his mouth.
Glowing coals flew out from him.

He split the sky and came down.
Heavy darkness lay under his feet.

He rode on a winged guardian{e} and flew.
He swooped down upon the wind’s wings.

He wrapped darkness around himself like a tent,
with dark water and thick storm clouds.

From the glow in front of him,
flames of fire blazed up.

Yahweh thundered from the sky.
The Most High raised his voice.

He shot arrows and scattered his enemies.
He flashed lightning and threw them into a panic.

The deep sea floor came into view.
The base of the world was uncovered
when Yahweh roared,
when the wind blasted from his nose.

“He stretched out his hand from on high and took hold of me.
He drew me up from the deep waters.

He saved me from a powerful enemy,
from haters who were stronger than I was.

They attacked me on my day of disaster,
but Yahweh held me up.

He brought me out into open space.
He saved me because I please him.

“Yahweh rewarded me for doing right.
He paid me back for my clean hands.

I have followed Yahweh’s paths.
I never turned against my God to do evil.

All his laws were before my eyes.
I never pushed his commands aside.

I lived without fault in his presence
and kept myself from sin.

So Yahweh has rewarded my righteousness,
and my innocence in his sight.

“You are loyal to the loyal.
You are honest with the honest.

You are pure toward the pure,
but you outwit the crooked.

You rescue the humble,
but you look at the proud and bring them down.

Yahweh, you are my lamp.
You turn my darkness into light.

With your help I can charge an army.
With my God I can jump a wall.

God’s way is flawless.
Yahweh’s promise is tested and true.
He is a shield for everyone who hides in him.

“Who is God except Yahweh?
Who is a rock besides us? Only our God!

This God is my powerful stronghold,{f}
and he makes my path safe.{g}

He gives me feet as quick as a deer’s.
He sets me on the high places.

He teaches my fingers to fight,
until my arms can stretch a bronze bow.

You gave me your saving shield,
and your care{h} has made me great.

You cleared a wide path for my steps,
so my ankles never gave way.

I hunted my enemies and destroyed them.
I turned back only when they were gone.

I wiped them out. I crushed them, and they could not get up.
They lay beneath my feet.

You clothed me with strength for the fight.
You forced my attackers to kneel before me.

You made my enemies run from me,
and I ended those who hated me.

They looked around, but no one came to help.
They cried to Yahweh, but he gave no reply.

I ground them down to powder like the dust of the ground.
I trampled them like mud in the street.

Foreigners crawl before me.
As soon as they hear about me, they do as I say.

Foreigners lose heart.
They come trembling{j} out of their forts.

“Yahweh lives! Praise my rock!
Lift high the God who is the rock of my rescue.

He is the God who pays back my enemies
and puts nations under my rule.

He sets me free from those who hate me.
You raise me high above those who attack me.
You save me from the violent man.

So, Yahweh, I will thank you among the nations.
I will sing to your name.

notes.text: This song is nearly the same as Psalm 18, with many small differences in wording.
“Horn” stands for strength.
Hebrew “belial,” meaning worthlessness or destruction.
Hebrew “Sheol,” the realm of the dead.
Hebrew “cherub,” a winged heavenly being.
So the Hebrew. Psalm 18:32 reads “who wraps me in strength,” and the Greek Old Testament here reads “who strengthens me with power.”
The Hebrew is uncertain. Perhaps “and made my way blameless” (compare Psalm 18:32), as in the Greek Old Testament.
Or “your humility” or “your gentleness.” Psalm 18:35 reads “your gentleness.”
So the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament and Psalm 18:43 read “the people.”
So Psalm 18:45. The Hebrew here reads “girded themselves” (uncertain).
So the traditional reading (qere), matching Psalm 18:50, “great salvation.” The written text reads “tower.”

verses.text:
These are the final words of David: “Here is the declaration of David, Jesse’s son,
the declaration of the man God set on high,
the king chosen by Jacob’s God,
the sweet poet of Israel’s songs.{a}

The Spirit of Yahweh spoke through me.
His word was on my tongue.

The God of Israel spoke.
The Rock of Israel told me:
‘A ruler who governs people with fairness,
who governs with respect for God,

is like the light at sunrise,
like a cloudless morning,
like fresh green grass that sprouts from the ground
after the sun comes out following the rain.’

“Is that not how God sees my family?
He made a lasting agreement with me,
complete in every part and firmly guarded.
Will he not make all my rescue and all my hopes flourish?{b}

But the worthless people{c} are like thorns that are thrown away,
because no one can pick them up with bare hands.

Whoever has to touch them arms himself with an iron tool or a spear shaft,
and the thorns are burned up right where they lie.”{d}

Here are the names of David’s champions. Josheb-basshebeth the Tahchemonite{e} headed the three.{f} He was Adino the Eznite. In a single fight he lifted his spear{g} against eight hundred enemies and cut them down.
Next came Eleazar, son of Dodo, descendant of Ahoah. He was one of the three warriors with David when they taunted the Philistines who had gathered for battle. The other Israelites had pulled back.
Eleazar held his ground and killed Philistines until his arm was exhausted and his hand was stuck to his sword. Yahweh gave a great victory that day. The army returned to him only to strip the dead.
After him came Shammah, Agee’s son, from Harar. Once the Philistines massed at Lehi,{h} where a lentil field lay. The Israelite troops fled from the Philistines.
But Shammah took a stand in the center of the plot and protected it. He struck down the Philistines, and Yahweh won a great victory.
At harvest time, three of the thirty leading soldiers went down to meet David at the cave of Adullam. A Philistine unit had set up camp in the Valley of Rephaim.
David himself was in the hideout then, and a Philistine garrison held Bethlehem.
David became very thirsty and sighed, “I wish someone would fetch me a drink from the well beside Bethlehem’s gate!”

So the three champions burst through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well beside Bethlehem’s gate, and took it to David. He refused to drink. Instead he poured it out on the ground in honor of Yahweh
and said, “Yahweh, I cannot possibly drink this! These men risked their lives, so this is like drinking their blood.” So he would not drink it. Such were the feats of the three champions.
Abishai, Joab’s brother, the son of Zeruiah, commanded the thirty.{i} Once he raised his spear against three hundred and killed every one. That made him as famous as the three.
Among the thirty he was the best regarded.{j} He became their commander, but he was never one of the three.

Next, Benaiah, the son of Jehoiada, came from Kabzeel and was a courageous man{k} with a record of great deeds. He killed two top fighters of Moab.{l} One snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion in it.
He also struck down an Egyptian of enormous size.{m} The Egyptian held a spear, while Benaiah had only a staff. He yanked the spear out of the Egyptian’s hand and ran him through with it.
Such were the achievements of Benaiah, Jehoiada’s son. He won fame alongside the three champions.
He was held in higher honor than the thirty, but he never joined the three. David made him head of his royal guard.{n}
The thirty included Joab’s brother Asahel, Elhanan son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
Shammah from Harod, Elika from Harod,
Helez from Palti, Ira, son of Ikkesh from Tekoa,
Abiezer from Anathoth, Mebunnai from Hushah,
Zalmon from Ahoah, Maharai from Netophah,
Heleb son of Baanah of Netophah, Ittai son of Ribai of Gibeah in Benjamin’s land,
Benaiah from Pirathon, Hiddai from the valleys of Gaash,
Abi-albon from Arabah, Azmaveth from Bahurim,
Eliahba from Shaalbon, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,{o}
Shammah from Harar, Ahiam, son of Sharar from Harar,
Eliphelet, son of Ahasbai from Maacah, Eliam, son of Ahithophel from Giloh,
Hezro from Carmel, Paarai from Arab,
Igal, son of Nathan from Zobah, Bani from Gad,
Zelek from Ammon, Naharai from Beeroth, who carried the armor of Joab, son of Zeruiah,
Ira from Jattir, Gareb from Jattir,
and Uriah the Hittite. In all there were thirty-seven.{p}

notes.text: Or “the favorite of Israel’s songs,” or “the joy of the Strong One of Israel” (uncertain). The Greek Old Testament reads “and beautiful are the psalms of Israel.”
Or as a statement: “For he will make all my rescue and all my hopes sprout.”
Hebrew “sons of Belial,” meaning worthless people.
Hebrew “in the sitting” (uncertain). Perhaps “on the spot.”

Josheb-basshebeth probably means “one who sits in the seat” (uncertain). First Chronicles 11:11 reads “Jashobeam, a Hachmonite.” The Greek Old Testament reads “Jebosthe the Canaanite,” which may reflect Ishbosheth or Ishbaal (compare 2:8).
So the traditional reading (qere). The written text reads “the captain” or “of the third ones.”

The Hebrew phrase “He was Adino the Eznite” is uncertain. First Chronicles 11:11 has “He raised his spear against three hundred men,” and the Greek Old Testament reads “he drew his sword against eight hundred.”
Lehi means “jawbone” (compare Judges 15:9). It may also mean “in a troop.”
So the Hebrew. Two Hebrew copies and the Syriac version read “of the thirty.”
Or “more honored than the three” (uncertain). Compare 1 Chronicles 11:21.
So the traditional reading (qere). The written text reads “a living man.”
Ariel probably means “lion of God” (uncertain). The Hebrew reads only “the two Ariel of Moab,” which may mean “two champions of Moab.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the two sons of Ariel of Moab.”
Hebrew “a man of appearance.” First Chronicles 11:23 says he was about 7½ feet (2.3 meters) tall, “five cubits.”
Hebrew “those who listen to him.” They may have been a private council.
The Hebrew is uncertain. First Chronicles 11:34 reads “the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan, son of Shagee.”
The list names fewer than thirty-seven. The total probably includes the leaders in verses 8-23 and Joab (uncertain).

verses.text: Again Yahweh was angry with Israel. He urged David to turn against them: “Take a census of Israel and Judah.”{a}

The king instructed Joab, his army commander, who was at his side, “Travel through every tribe of Israel, from Dan in the far north down to Beersheba, and enroll the population. I want to know their total.”
Joab said to the king, “May Yahweh your God make the nation a hundred times bigger than it is, and may your own eyes see it, my lord the king. Yet why does my lord want this?”
But the king’s command prevailed over Joab and the officers. They left the king to take the census of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and set up camp at Aroer, south of the town in the center of the Gad valley. From there they continued toward Jazer.
Next they visited Gilead and the area of Tahtim-hodshi,{b} then Dan-jaan, and they circled around toward Sidon.
They also reached the fortified city of Tyre and every town of the Hivites and Canaanites. Last, they came to Beersheba, in Judah’s southern desert.
They toured the entire land and returned to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days.
Joab handed the king the census figures: 800,000 trained swordsmen in Israel and 500,000 men in Judah.{c}
David felt guilty after he had counted the fighting men. He said to Yahweh, “I have committed a terrible sin by doing this. Now, Yahweh, I beg you to forgive my guilt. I was very foolish.”
Before David rose the next morning, Yahweh’s message had reached the prophet Gad, David’s seer.
“Go to David and say, ‘This is what Yahweh declares: I offer you three punishments. Select one, and I will bring it on you.’”

Gad came to David and reported this. “Which will it be?” he asked. “Seven{d} years of hunger across your land? Three months of fleeing while your enemies hunt you down? Or three days of deadly illness in the land? Consider it, and tell me the answer to take back to the one who sent me.”
“This is a painful choice,” David told Gad. “Let Yahweh be the one to punish us, since he is very merciful. Do not let people be the ones.”
Yahweh sent a plague on Israel. It began that morning and lasted for the period he had decided.{e} Seventy thousand people died, from one end of the country to the other.

The angel raised his arm over Jerusalem to wipe it out. Yahweh felt sorrow over the disaster and told the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Lower your hand.” At that moment the angel of Yahweh was beside the threshing floor of Araunah{f} the Jebusite.
When David saw the angel killing the people, he cried out to Yahweh, “I am the guilty one! I did the wrong. What have these sheep done? Strike me instead, and strike my father’s family.”
That day Gad visited David and said, “Climb up to the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and set up an altar to Yahweh there.”
David went up, as Gad had told him to do, following Yahweh’s command.
When Araunah glanced over, he spotted the king and his men walking toward him. He hurried out and bowed low, his face touching the ground.
“Why is my lord the king visiting me?” Araunah asked. David said, “I want to purchase your threshing floor and build Yahweh an altar there, so that the plague will end.”
Araunah told David, “My lord the king, take it and offer whatever you like. Here are oxen for the burnt offering. The threshing boards and the ox yokes can be the firewood.
Your Majesty, Araunah is giving the king all of it.”{g} Then he said, “May Yahweh your God be pleased with you.”
The king answered, “No, I must pay a price. I refuse to give Yahweh my God offerings that cost me nothing.” So he paid about 20 ounces of silver{h} for the threshing floor and the oxen.
There David built Yahweh an altar and presented burnt offerings and fellowship offerings.{i} Yahweh answered the prayer for the land, and the plague on Israel stopped.

notes.text: Compare 1 Chronicles 21:1, where Satan stirs David up.

The Hebrew is unclear. Tahtim-hodshi may mean “lowlands of Hodshi.” The Greek Old Testament reads “the land of Thabason, which is Adasai.” Some scholars change it to “Kadesh in the land of the Hittites.”
First Chronicles 21:5 gives 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah. The Greek Old Testament here agrees with the Hebrew of Samuel.
So the Hebrew. The Greek Old Testament and 1 Chronicles 21:12 read “three.”
Or “until the time of the assembly” (uncertain). The Greek Old Testament reads “from morning until noon” and adds that it was the time of the wheat harvest.

So the traditional reading (qere). The spelling of the name varies in this chapter. First Chronicles 21:15 calls him Ornan, and the Greek Old Testament reads “Orna.” The name may be Hurrian, perhaps a title meaning “lord” (uncertain).
Or “All this, O king, Araunah gives to the king.” Some readers take it as “Araunah the king,” which would mean he was once a Jebusite ruler.
Hebrew “fifty shekels,” about 20 ounces (575 grams). First Chronicles 21:25 reads “six hundred shekels of gold,” about 15 pounds (6.9 kilograms), for the whole site.
Hebrew “peace offerings.” The Greek Old Testament adds, “and Solomon made an addition to the altar afterward, for it was small at first.”
